analysis.one_liner: Bans lawsuits against makers and sellers of quartz and stone countertops for silica injuries to workers.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 16-7 in June 2026; it has not received a vote by the full House.
analysis.plain_summary: Cutting and polishing engineered stone countertops releases silica dust that can cause a serious, incurable lung disease. Workers who get sick have been suing the companies that make and sell the slabs. This bill would make those lawsuits illegal in every state and federal court, and would immediately throw out any such lawsuit already in progress.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers of stone slab products — companies that make or sell quartz, porcelain, glass, and ceramic slabs — would be shielded from civil lawsuits over injuries tied to cutting and shaping their products, and any pending lawsuits against them would be dismissed [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any civil action against a manufacturer or seller of a stone slab product for injuries arising from fabrication by another party, including injuries from exposure to respirable silica [S3].
Requires courts to dismiss any such lawsuit already pending when the bill becomes law [S2][S3].

The bill's stated purpose includes protecting manufacturers and sellers from suits over injuries caused by third-party fabricators they do not control, and preserving the industry and consumer supply of stone slabs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who cut, grind, and polish the slabs — the people exposed to silica dust on the job — would lose the right to sue the manufacturers and sellers of the products that made them sick, in any court, and pending cases would be wiped out. Their recovery would be limited to whatever workers' compensation provides [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill completely bars injured workers' claims against manufacturers and sellers, with no exception, and applies retroactively to dismiss lawsuits already filed [S2][S3].

Fabrication shops — often small businesses — would remain the only parties workers can sue, even though the bill's own findings acknowledge some fabricators violate workplace safety rules [S3]; the bill shifts the legal target without reducing the underlying hazard.

Respirable crystalline silica, the substance the bill names, is a well-documented cause of silicosis, an incurable and often fatal lung disease; eliminating lawsuits removes one of the main financial pressures on producers to make safer products.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The industry argument has some force: a slab maker that ships a finished product has limited control over how a downstream fabrication shop handles it, and workplace safety rules do govern fabrication. But this bill does not merely clarify who is responsible — it eliminates the claim entirely, for every manufacturer and seller, in every court, and retroactively kills cases already filed. The entire cost of that shield falls on workers with a serious occupational lung disease, while the companies that profit from the product pay nothing. A narrower bill (for example, one with exceptions) was not what the committee approved.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill on a 16-7 vote on June 3, 2026, and it is now waiting for a vote by the full House, which has not been scheduled [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Tom McClintock introduced the bill on September 17, 2025, with Rep. Andy Biggs of Arizona, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S3].
Sixteen House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee held a markup session and ordered the bill reported, as amended, by a vote of 16 to 7 [S5].
The bill has not been taken up by the full House; the Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so a floor vote remains possible [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the outcome is unsettled: stone slab manufacturers and importers are better off than they were before the committee vote, since a shield from silicosis lawsuits has advanced one step, while workers who have sued retain their rights only because the bill has not yet passed.

industries.industry: Engineered stone slab manufacturers, importers, and sellers
industries.note: The bill would permanently bar lawsuits over silica injuries linked to fabricating their products and dismiss pending cases [S2][S3]. Engineered stone is typically more than 90% silica, so cutting it releases the dust at the heart of these claims; the shield removes both the companies' court exposure and a market pressure to make safer products.

These small businesses are not protected — they would remain the only defendants workers can sue [S3]. They neither gain nor lose liability under the bill; they simply carry it alone while manufacturers walk away.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' attorneys handling silica and toxic-tort cases
industries.note: A whole category of claims would become illegal to file, eliminating this line of work; their interest here runs alongside injured workers' access to court.

analysis.trajectory: Bills reported from committee still need a scheduled floor vote in the House, then passage in the Senate, before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027. With all-Republican sponsorship and no floor action scheduled, the bill's most likely path is stalling unless its supporters attach the liability shield to a larger bill moving through Congress.
